title: SYSK Selects: How Trickle-Down Economics Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of an episode on trickle-down economics. Hosts explain the term's origins (Will Rogers, 1920s; George H.W. Bush's "voodoo economics" jab at Reagan), the link to supply-side economics and Reaganomics, and the contrast with Say's Law and Keynesian demand-side thinking. They cover Laffer curve and the prohibitive range, the argument that wealthy people may hoard rather than invest, a fair Economy analysis showing little correlation between top tax rates and growth, Thomas Sowell's objection to the term, Obama-era quantitative easing as "trickle down monetary policy," and a closing debate on estate taxes and inheritance. The hosts repeatedly say economics is not settled and that the evidence is disputed. Listener mail from Caleb about dental school applications closes the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and Ferris Bueller's voodoo economics
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode with off-topic banter, then recalls Ben Stein's economics professor role in Ferris Bueller's Day Off and George H.W. Bush coining 'voodoo economics' for Reagan's policies. They note economics is not a science and that the topic is hard to settle.

segments.title: Definition and origins of trickle-down economics
segments.summary: The hosts define trickle-down economics as transferring wealth to the wealthiest so they reinvest and benefit others. They note the term predates the 1980s, traced to a Will Rogers quote in the 1920s, and that supporters dislike the label, preferring supply-side economics.

segments.title: Supply versus demand, Say's law and Keynes
segments.summary: The hosts explain Jean-Baptiste Say's idea that products are paid for with products and how the 'supply creates its own demand' version is a misreading. They discuss housing glut examples, Jefferson's agreement, and the shift to Keynesian demand-side thinking.

segments.title: Early supply-side policy, Hoover and the Great Depression
segments.summary: Harding and Coolidge used supply-side tax cuts, and Hoover continued them before the Great Depression. Roosevelt followed Keynes's demand-focused approach, and the hosts describe later presidents such as Kennedy and Reagan embracing supply-side ideas.

segments.title: Laffer curve and the prohibitive range
segments.summary: The hosts explain the Laffer curve as a thought experiment relating tax rates to revenue, with a prohibitive range where high taxes reduce work incentives and revenue can fall. They give a worked example of a business owner or salaried employee deciding not to take more income.

segments.title: Hoarding, inequality and the case against trickle-down
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether wealthy people actually reinvest, noting that people may hoard money out of fear, and that recession-era bargains favor the rich. They cite Thomas Sowell's objection to the term and a fair Economy analysis finding little statistical link between top tax rate cuts and GDP, wages or unemployment.

segments.title: Reaganomics results and Obama's quantitative easing
segments.summary: The hosts say evaluations of Reaganomics disagree and that inflation and revenue effects are contested. They argue Obama-era quantitative easing can be seen as trickle-down monetary policy, benefiting the wealthy.

segments.title: Estate taxes, inheritance and dynasties
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether high estate taxes should replace high income taxes on the wealthy, arguing inherited wealth is invested less than earned wealth. Josh disagrees on government role, and they conclude with personal views on wealth and self-sufficiency.

segments.title: Listener mail: Caleb and the waiting game
segments.summary: Caleb from Indiana writes that the podcast helps him cope while waiting on dental school applications, and asks for a shout-out to his fiancée Elizabeth.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact info and website details and sign off.
